title: Pressure Pulsar: Kp and Partial Pressures
welcome_lead: Apply Kp to gas-phase equilibria using partial pressures and mole fractions.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on Kp and gaseous equilibrium calculations.
final_note: You wielded partial pressures to master Kp.

concepts.def: Pressure of one gas in a mixture.
Moles of gas / total gas moles.

walkthroughs.body_html:
p(A) = x(A) × P_total, where x(A) = n(A) / n_total. Mole fractions must sum to 1.

For 2 mol N2 and 6 mol H2 in 10 mol mixture at 100 kPa: p(N2) = 20 kPa, p(H2) = 60 kPa.

Same form as Kc but use partial pressures: Kp = p(C)^c p(D)^d / p(A)^a p(B)^b.

Solids and liquids are omitted. Example: CaCO3(s) <-> CaO(s) + CO2(g) gives Kp = p(CO2).

Add powers of pressure in numerator minus denominator: Δn = (c+d) - (a+b).

If Δn = 0, Kp is unitless. For Haber (Δn = -2), units are Pa^-2 or kPa^-2.

mcqs.q: Sum of mole fractions in mixture?
What does Kp use instead of concentrations?
options: Kp uses the volumes of each gas in the mixture.
Kp uses the total pressure of the system raised to the stoichiometric coefficients.
Partial pressures of each gaseous component at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: What are the units of Kc for a reaction?
options: A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.
They depend on Δn (the difference between moles of gaseous/aqueous products and reactants) — Kc can be dimensionless or have units like mol dm^-3.
Kc always has units of mol dm^-3.

mcqs.q: Does adding a catalyst change the value of Kc?
options: A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.
No — a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so Kc is unchanged.
Kp uses the volumes of each gas in the mixture.
A catalyst increases Kc by favouring product formation.
